title: Bengal orders police to use hospital-violence law after clash at Calcutta Medical College
dek: The health department has told district magistrates and police chiefs to book attacks on doctors and hospitals under a 2009 law with a three-year jail term, days after a sit-in by interns ended in violence.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
West Bengal's health department has told police across the state to register attacks on doctors, nurses and hospitals under a 2009 law that carries up to three years in jail, rather than treat them as ordinary disorder, days after a sit-in by interns at Calcutta Medical College and Hospital ended in a violent clash on Wednesday night.

The instructions, sent to all district magistrates, superintendents of police and police commissioners, including Kolkata's, direct police to register cases as soon as a complaint is received, begin investigating without delay and preserve CCTV footage, documents and medical evidence, according to reports. The order invokes the West Bengal Medicare Service Persons and Medicare Service Institutions (Prevention of Violence and Damage to Property) Act, 2009, under which offences are cognisable and non-bailable.

## What the order says

Physical assaults, threats, intimidation, obstruction of duty and damage to hospital buildings, equipment or furniture must be handled under the 2009 Act and "must not be treated merely as cases of general disorder", the department said, according to reports. Offenders can be jailed for up to three years, fined up to ₹50,000 and made to pay compensation for damage to hospital property.

Hospitals are told to tighten security at government hospitals and other health institutions, with particular attention to emergency departments, casualty wards and intensive care units, where confrontations with patients' families are most common. The order has not been published on the department's website, and The Declaration has not seen its text; its contents are as described in reports. It does not name any incident, but reports link it directly to the violence at Calcutta Medical College.

## What happened at Calcutta Medical College

The clash grew out of a dispute that began after the Chorbagan Durga Puja stampede in north Kolkata in October, which killed 19 people and injured at least 25. Interns at Calcutta Medical College spoke to reporters after the crush, questioning the decision to move seriously injured victims to a private hospital and alleging shortages of medicines and emergency supplies. Reports differ on the date of that press conference.

The health department later issued show-cause notices to eight interns, accusing them of speaking to the media during duty hours and of making claims about shortages that it said were baseless. The department has denied any shortage and has defended the transfers as a way to give patients better treatment.

On Wednesday, 18 November, interns and junior doctors staged a sit-in outside the principal's office in the administrative block, demanding that the notices be withdrawn. At about 7.30 pm a group entered the campus through the main gate and approached the building, and the confrontation lasted about two and a half hours, according to reports. Students locked themselves inside the administrative building, window panes were broken and parts of the building damaged, and the principal was escorted out by police at about 10.45 pm, students said, according to reports.

Several interns and junior doctors were injured. Six junior doctors suffered head injuries, one report said, and one final-year student was reported to be in a serious condition. Patients' relatives in the hospital at the time were also caught up in the violence, reports said. The health minister said two professors had been assaulted.

Police registered a case on their own initiative against unidentified people the next day and are examining CCTV footage, according to reports. No arrests had been reported by Saturday night.

## What each side says

Accounts of who was responsible differ sharply, and none of the allegations has been established.

Protesting doctors say the attackers were outsiders who carried sticks and threw stones, and that police stood by. "The police stood by as mute spectators," one junior doctor said, according to reports. The West Bengal Junior Doctors' Front and the Joint Platform of Doctors allege that people linked to the BJP, the RSS and its student wing, the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP), were involved. Some of the men who entered the campus identified themselves to reporters as members of the ABVP and the National Medicos Organisation, according to one report; neither organisation has made a formal statement on that claim.

The ABVP denies attacking anyone. Its South Bengal state secretary, Nilkantha Bhattacharya, said Left-wing students had surrounded the principal's chamber and that the secretary of its college unit had been seriously injured, according to reports. Earlier the same day, members of the ABVP and the Left-aligned Students' Federation of India (SFI) had clashed over a bookstall on College Street, near the University of Calcutta.

Health Minister Sharadwat Mukherjee said "10-15 outsiders", claiming to speak for the college's roughly 1,250 interns, had organised the unrest, assaulted two professors and damaged property. He blamed "Naxalite elements" and described some of the protesters as "mentally Maoists and Naxalites", according to reports. He said CCTV footage of the whole incident was available and that legal action would be taken against anyone who had entered the campus to cause trouble. He has defended the show-cause notices as following National Medical Commission rules.

Doctors' groups rejected the minister's description. Punyabrata Goon, convenor of the Joint Platform of Doctors, questioned the labelling of protesters as Maoists and a warning that doctors' registrations could be cancelled, according to reports. Debasish Halder of the Junior Doctors' Front alleged that the notices had been issued on the instructions of "higher authorities" without the college holding its own inquiry.

## The inquiry

The health department has set up a three-member committee to investigate the violence. It can seek help from Kolkata Police and examine CCTV footage and photographs, according to reports. The two doctors' platforms say the panel cannot be impartial because it has no representative of the protesting doctors. The committee's members and deadline have not been made public.

## Background

The 2009 Act dates from the Left Front government's final years in office. Violence in hospitals became a national issue in Bengal in August 2024, when a mob vandalised RG Kar Medical College and Hospital during protests over the rape and murder of a trainee doctor there. The Calcutta High Court called that episode a failure of the state machinery, and junior doctors went on a long strike demanding better security.

Some leaders of the 2024 movement are again prominent in the protest at Calcutta Medical College. Mr Halder, one of them, called the show-cause notices "political revenge" earlier this week, according to reports. The present government, led by Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari of the BJP, took office in May. Mr Adhikari has said it should be examined whether the interns were on duty when they spoke to reporters, according to reports.

## What happens next

The interns' replies to the show-cause notices, and any decision on them, are the next step in the original dispute. The three-member committee's findings will decide whether the government blames students, outsiders or both for Wednesday's violence. Whether the new instructions change police practice will show in how cases from Wednesday night are registered: under the 2009 Act, or under general law.
